content: Reducing the transmission of SARS-CoV-2 is a global priority. Contact tracing is a critical public health measure that identifies individuals who have recently been in contact with an infected person, enabling their isolation to prevent further spread of the virus. Digital technologies have the potential to enhance and expedite traditional manual contact tracing efforts. These digital tools can be categorized into three main areas: outbreak response, proximity tracing, and symptom tracking. A rapid review was conducted to evaluate the effectiveness of digital contact tracing solutions during infectious disease outbreaks. The objective was to assess the benefits, harms, and acceptability of personal digital contact tracing tools in identifying contacts of confirmed cases of infectious diseases. The literature search spanned from January 1, 2000, to May 5, 2020, and included databases such as CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and Embase, as well as the Cochrane COVID-19 Study Register. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs), cluster-RCTs, quasi-RCTs, cohort studies, cross-sectional studies, and modeling studies. Studies focusing on contact tracing during outbreaks of diseases like COVID-19, Ebola, tuberculosis, SARS, and MERS were prioritized as direct evidence. Comparative studies of contact tracing outside outbreak settings were considered as indirect evidence. Digital contact tracing solutions typically involved software or firmware installed on personal devices or provided by governments or third parties. These were compared to traditional methods such as manual contact tracing, self-reported diaries, surveys, interviews, and other standard approaches. The outcomes assessed included the identification of secondary cases and close contacts, the time required to complete contact tracing, issues of acceptability and accessibility, privacy and safety concerns, and other ethical considerations. Two reviewers independently screened records and full-text publications. Data extraction was divided equally between two reviewers, with cross-checking for accuracy. The quality of included studies was assessed using GRADE-CERQual for qualitative data and GRADE for modeling and cohort studies. Modeling studies provided estimates of the effects of different contact tracing solutions, while cohort studies offered empirically measured outcomes. The review identified six cohort studies with quantitative data and six modeling studies simulating digital contact tracing solutions. Two cohort studies also included qualitative data. Three cohort studies examined contact tracing during actual outbreaks, while the other three simulated outbreak scenarios in non-outbreak settings, such as schools. Of the six modeling studies, four focused on COVID-19 scenarios, and two simulated close contacts in non-specific outbreak settings. Findings from Modeling Studies: Two modeling studies provided low-certainty evidence that digital contact tracing could reduce secondary cases, measured as the effective reproductive number (Reff). One study estimated an 18% reduction in Reff with digital contact tracing compared to self-isolation alone, and a 35% reduction with manual contact tracing. Another study found a 26% reduction in Reff with digital contact tracing compared to self-isolation alone, and a 53% reduction with manual contact tracing compared to self-isolation alone. However, the certainty of these findings was limited due to unclear model specifications, assumptions about the effectiveness of manual contact tracing (assumed to trace 95-100% of contacts), and assumptions about app adoption rates (53% of the population). Findings from Cohort Studies: Two cohort studies provided very low-certainty evidence suggesting that digital contact tracing may identify more close contacts than manual methods. During an Ebola outbreak, app-based contact tracers identified twice as many close contacts per case compared to those using paper forms. In a pertussis outbreak in a U.S. hospital, radio-frequency identification identified 45 close contacts, whereas electronic medical record searches identified only 13. One cohort study provided very low-certainty evidence that digital tools could reduce the time required to complete contact tracing. Digital data entry and management systems were reported to be faster and less prone to data loss compared to paper-based systems. In two studies from loweror middle-income countries, contact tracing teams found digital systems easier to use, more accurate for handling large datasets, and more portable than paper systems. However, these benefits were offset by increased costs and challenges with internet access. Privacy concerns were noted, as devices appeared to protect user privacy from contacts, but risks of privacy breaches, such as linkage attacks, were identified, particularly with wearable devices. Conclusions: The effectiveness of digital contact tracing solutions remains largely unproven due to limited real-world data. Modeling studies provide low-certainty evidence that digital contact tracing, when combined with other public health measures like self-isolation, may reduce secondary cases. Cohort studies provide very low-certainty evidence that digital tools may improve the accuracy of contact identification and reduce the time required for contact tracing. However, digital solutions may exacerbate inequities for populations with limited internet access or digital technology. Stronger primary research is needed to evaluate the effectiveness of digital contact tracing technologies, particularly in real-world outbreak settings. Future studies should explore the integration of digital and manual systems, as digital solutions are unlikely to be used in isolation. Research should also prioritize the acceptability and accessibility of digital tools, as privacy concerns and other barriers may hinder their adoption and effectiveness.
